label: Steps a day
body:
Heart and longevity benefits climb
steeply up to about 8,000 steps.
No gym needed. A 10-min walk after
meals also blunts sugar spikes.
caption:
You don't need 10,000 steps. But you probably need more than you're doing.

The 10k number came from a 1960s pedometer ad — not science.

What large studies actually show: the risk of early death drops steeply as daily steps rise, and the benefit starts levelling off around 7,000–8,000 steps for most adults.

Easy ways to get there:
→ 10-minute walk after each meal
→ Take calls standing or walking
→ Stairs instead of the lift
→ Park or get off one stop early

Walking is the most underrated health habit there is.

label: Nutrition
headline:
Vitamin D
in India
body: Most Indians are deficient despite the sun. Signs: fatigue, body aches, weak bones. Get 15–20 min of midday sun on arms and legs, and get tested.
caption:
India gets more sunshine than most countries. So why are most Indians low on vitamin D?

Indoor jobs, covered clothing, pollution and darker skin all cut how much your skin makes.

What low vitamin D can feel like:
→ Constant tiredness
→ Aching bones and muscles
→ Low mood
→ Getting sick often

What helps:
→ 15–20 min of midday sun on arms and legs, a few times a week
→ Eggs, fatty fish, fortified milk
→ A simple blood test — and a supplement only if your doctor says so

Don't guess. Test.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Fruit juice is
healthy?
body: Packaged juice has nearly as much sugar as a cola, and almost none of the fibre. Eat the whole fruit — it keeps you full and your blood sugar steady.
caption:
That "100% natural" juice box isn't the health drink it looks like.

Juicing strips out the fibre — the part that slows sugar down.

One 250 ml glass of packaged juice has roughly 20–25 g of sugar. A can of cola has about 27 g.

What happens without the fibre:
→ Sugar hits your blood fast
→ You're hungry again soon
→ It's easy to drink 3 oranges' worth in 30 seconds

The swap: eat the whole fruit. Same vitamins, plus fibre, plus actually feeling full.

label: Caffeine cutoff
body:
Caffeine has a ~5 hour half-life.
A 5 PM chai is still working
at 10 PM, cutting deep sleep.
Keep tea & coffee before 2 PM.
caption:
Sleeping badly even though you're exhausted? Check when you had your last chai.

Caffeine has a half-life of about 5 hours.

That means half the caffeine from a 5 PM coffee is still in your system at 10 PM — and some of it is still there at midnight.

Even if you fall asleep fine, late caffeine:
→ Reduces deep sleep
→ Makes sleep lighter and more broken
→ Leaves you groggy the next morning
→ So you reach for more caffeine… and repeat

The fix: keep tea and coffee before 2 PM. Switch to herbal tea after.

label: Reality check
headline:
Veg diet covers
every nutrient?
body: B12 comes almost only from animal foods. Many Indian vegetarians run low — tingling hands, fatigue, brain fog. Get tested and supplement if needed.
caption:
A vegetarian diet can be incredibly healthy. But there's one nutrient it struggles with.

Vitamin B12.

B12 is found almost entirely in animal foods — meat, fish, eggs, and smaller amounts in milk and curd. Plants don't make it.

Signs your B12 might be low:
→ Constant tiredness and weakness
→ Tingling or numbness in hands and feet
→ Brain fog and poor memory
→ Pale skin, breathlessness

What to do:
→ Include milk, curd, paneer daily
→ Get a B12 blood test
→ Supplement if your doctor recommends it

label: Training
headline:
Start strength
training
body: Two full-body sessions of squats, push-ups, rows and lunges build muscle, protect joints and improve blood sugar. Start with bodyweight.
caption:
Strength training isn't just for bodybuilders. It's one of the best things you can do for long-term health.

And you need far less than you think.

WHO recommends muscle-strengthening work at least 2 days a week. That's it.

What it does for you:
→ Builds and keeps muscle as you age
→ Stronger bones and joints
→ Better blood sugar control
→ Higher resting metabolism

A simple start: squats, push-ups (wall or knee is fine), rows, lunges. 2–3 sets each, twice a week.

label: Did you know
headline:
Rest days
build muscle.
body: Muscle grows while you recover, not while you lift. Training the same muscle hard every day just piles up fatigue. Give it about 48 hours.
caption:
Training hard every single day and not seeing results? You might need less, not more.

Lifting creates tiny damage in your muscles. They grow back stronger while you rest — not during the workout.

Skip recovery and you get:
→ Stalled strength
→ Constant soreness
→ Poor sleep and low energy
→ Higher injury risk

The rule of thumb: about 48 hours before training the same muscle group hard again. Walking and stretching on rest days is great.

Recovery is part of the program.

label: Max salt per day
body:
WHO's limit: under 5 g — about 1 tsp.
Most Indians eat far more.
Pickles, papad, namkeen & sauces
are the hidden sources.
caption:
You probably eat way more salt than you think — and most of it isn't from the salt shaker.

WHO recommends less than 5 g of salt a day. That's about one teaspoon, in total.

Studies show average intake in India is well above that.

Where the hidden salt comes from:
→ Pickles and papad
→ Namkeen, chips and biscuits
→ Sauces, ketchup and instant noodles
→ Restaurant and packaged food

Why it matters: too much salt raises blood pressure — a major cause of heart attacks and strokes.

label: Nutrition
headline:
Fibre, the
forgotten one
body: Keeps you full, feeds your gut bacteria and steadies blood sugar. Easy wins: whole dal and chana, fruit with skin, veggies at every meal, oats.
caption:
Everyone talks about protein. Almost no one talks about fibre — and most people don't get nearly enough.

The target for adults: around 25–30 g a day.

Why it matters:
→ Keeps you full longer (helps with weight)
→ Steadies blood sugar after meals
→ Feeds the good bacteria in your gut
→ Helps lower cholesterol

Easy Indian sources:
→ Whole dal, rajma, chana
→ Fruit with the skin on (guava, apple, pear)
→ A vegetable with every meal
→ Oats, whole wheat roti, millets

label: Myth buster
headline:
Skipping meals
burns more fat?
body: Fat loss comes from your overall calorie balance, not missed meals. Skipping often leads to overeating later. Pick a meal pattern you can actually stick to.
caption:
Skipping lunch to "save calories" and then raiding the kitchen at 6 PM? You're not alone.

There's nothing magic about skipping meals.

Fat loss comes down to your overall calorie balance across days and weeks. Two meals or five — it works the same if the total is the same.

What skipping often does instead:
→ Big hunger later → overeating
→ Low energy and irritability
→ Cravings for fried and sugary food
→ Less protein across the day

The best eating pattern is the one you can stick to — with protein in every meal.

label: Active minutes a week
body:
WHO's minimum for adults:
150 min of moderate activity.
That's just 30 min, 5 days a week.
Brisk walking counts.
caption:
Think you need an hour at the gym every day to be healthy? You don't.

WHO's minimum for adults: 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.

That's 30 minutes, 5 days a week.

What counts as moderate (you can talk, but not sing):
→ Brisk walking
→ Cycling
→ Swimming
→ Dancing, sports, even vigorous housework

Add 2 days of strength training and you've hit the full recommendation.

Something is always better than nothing.

label: Reality check
headline:
Always tired?
It's just stress?
body: Not always. Low iron, B12, vitamin D or thyroid issues are common causes — especially in Indian women. A simple blood test can tell.
caption:
Tired all the time, even after sleeping? Don't just blame stress.

Ongoing fatigue often has a fixable cause.

Common ones worth checking:
→ Low iron / anaemia (very common in Indian women)
→ Low vitamin B12
→ Low vitamin D
→ Thyroid problems
→ Poor sleep quality

A basic blood panel — CBC, ferritin, B12, vitamin D, TSH — can rule most of these in or out.

If tiredness has lasted weeks, talk to a doctor. It's not "just how you are."

label: Sleep
headline:
Sleep better
tonight
body: Your body clock loves routine. Get morning sunlight, keep your room cool and dark, and put the phone away 30 minutes before bed.
caption:
Struggling to fall asleep — or waking up tired? The fix usually starts in the morning, not at night.

Your body clock runs on routine. The single most powerful habit: wake up at the same time every day, weekends included.

Then add:
→ 10 minutes of morning sunlight
→ No caffeine after 2 PM
→ A cool, dark, quiet room
→ Phone away 30 minutes before bed

Give it two weeks. Consistency beats any sleep gadget.

label: Did you know
headline:
Your resting
heart rate talks.
body: Normal is 60–100 bpm, and fitter people sit lower. If yours stays higher than usual for days, it can signal poor sleep, stress or illness.
caption:
Your resting heart rate is one of the simplest health signals you can track — and it's free.

Measure it in the morning, before getting out of bed.

What the numbers mean:
→ 60–100 bpm is the normal adult range
→ Regular exercise usually brings it lower over time
→ A rise of several beats for days can mean poor sleep, stress, dehydration or an oncoming illness

Track it for a week to learn your baseline. Changes matter more than one reading.

If it's often above 100 at rest, or you feel palpitations or dizziness, see a doctor.
